One thing to consider is that by the time most of these "old debts" get to the point of garnishment, none of that money goes to the original creditor. The bad debt is bought in bulk auctions for pennies (or fractions of pennies) of face value. Some law firms buy up and process these things by the thousands, receiving crazy returns on their "investment." An old debt with a judgment buried in a box with hundreds of others may have cost $1 or $2, or even far less, yet with a few hundred dollars of court filing fees the law firm seizes thousands of dollars from the debtor. True, they legally own it and have the power and right to do this, but I don't think that passing some legislation to limit this type of action would make credit more expensive, since the risk to the creditor remains the same as it is now. The ones who would be hit financially are these firms that earn their entire revenue from collecting on old bad debts.
